== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: High risk / High concern: Severe longitudinal loss to follow-up occurred in both sites—only 34% (287/843) of baseline households were retained in Mudaka (66% attrition) and 58% (513/890) in Panzi (42% attrition) due to local instability, displacement, and lack of formal addresses (PDF pp. 4-5, 7). No attrition balance table or statistical adjustment for missingness is presented, with attrition comparisons cited only as '(data not shown)' (PDF p. 7).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High risk / High concern: There is no unexposed comparison community and zero statistical adjustment for confounding. Quantitative analyses are restricted to unadjusted descriptive stratification and unsupervised k-means clustering of baseline wealth proxies analyzed separately by site (PDF p. 4), leaving associations between maternal education, household wealth proxies, and Asili service uptake wholly unadjusted (PDF p. 6).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / Low quality (private social-enterprise tariff/membership structure rather than statutory law): The intervention is an NGO/human-centered-design social enterprise franchise program (Asili) offering paid monthly memberships versus per-unit clinic and standpipe fees under community-level consent from the Mwami of Kabare (PDF pp. 2-3). Operationalization of contractual membership versus ad-hoc user status was compromised because respondents were confused about the difference between 'member' and 'user' (PDF p. 7), and exact monetary fee schedules were not reported.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High risk / High concern: Pre-specified primary child health outcomes (14-day maternal recall of diarrhea, cough, and fever, supplemented by medical charts) failed due to poor maternal recall in large households and inaccessible chart records and were omitted altogether (PDF pp. 4, 7). Follow-up Asili utilization and membership relied on unverified self-report afflicted by respondent confusion between 'user' and 'member' definitions (PDF p. 7), and focus group data collection/translation lacked documented rigor.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Low quality: Clean water standpipe and clinic utilization were captured solely through self-report at follow-up with documented misclassification between 'member' and 'user' categories (PDF p. 7). Objective water quality/supply metrics were absent, baseline drinking water and toilet type variables were omitted from cluster reporting due to lacking 'notable trends' (PDF p. 4), and primary child morbidity outcomes were dropped entirely due to poor data quality (PDF p. 4).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High risk / High concern: ClinicalTrials.gov registration (NCT03536286) was retrospective as of April 23, 2018—nearly two years after August 2016 baseline enrollment in Mudaka and right before May-August 2018 follow-up (PDF pp. 1, 3). Intended primary child morbidity outcomes were excluded from Results (PDF p. 4), cluster variables without 'notable trends' (drinking water and roofing material in Mudaka; toilet type in Mudaka and Panzi) were selectively omitted (PDF p. 4), and attrition comparisons were cited as '(data not shown)' (PDF p. 7).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High risk / High concern: Although baseline household enrollment systematically sampled every third or fourth household with under-five children across mapped sub-regions in Mudaka and Panzi (PDF p. 3), follow-up analyses suffered severe selection/attrition losses (66% in Mudaka, 42% in Panzi), excluded households with missing baseline cluster variables or unknown village data (PDF p. 4), and provided no recruitment criteria, sample sizes, or selection procedures for follow-up focus group participants (PDF p. 3).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its aim to evaluate community utilization of and response to the Asili social enterprise health clinic and clean water services in Mudaka and Panzi, South Kivu, DRC.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Baseline and follow-up household surveys paired with follow-up focus group discussions provided empirical data on Asili uptake across socioeconomic profiles and community perceptions of service quality and affordability (though pre-planned child morbidity data failed and were excluded).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 1 (Abstract: Methods); PDF Pages 3-4 (Methods: Data collection, Outcomes, Data analysis)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Focus group discussions with community members are an appropriate qualitative method to explore community acceptance, perceived child health benefits, and affordability barriers to a new social enterprise intervention.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 1 (Abstract); PDF Page 3 (Methods: Data collection)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper states only that 'additional community input was collected through small focus groups during follow-up' and that local staff assisted with translation, without reporting the number of focus groups, number or characteristics of participants, recruitment strategy, discussion guide, audio recording, or transcription procedures.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: No qualitative coding procedure, thematic analysis framework, or data verification method is described anywhere in the Methods section; Author Contributions merely notes that one author 'conducted all analysis of focus group interviews, including translation of French into English'.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 (Methods: Data analysis); PDF Page 7 (Author contributions)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: The qualitative interpretations—that clinic and water standpipe prices barred poorer families while users valued perceived care quality and cleaner water—are illustrated with brief direct participant quotes in Mudaka and Panzi, though without participant/group identifiers or breadth of theme coverage across groups.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: Because focus group sampling, data collection protocols, and qualitative coding/analytic methods are completely omitted from the Methods section, methodological coherence linking raw focus group data to final selected quotes cannot be verified.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 3 (Methods: Data collection); PDF Pages 4-6 (Results); PDF Page 7 (Author contributions)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.1: Are the participants representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: While baseline recruitment systematically sampled every third or fourth household with under-five children across mapped regions of Mudaka and Panzi, follow-up analyses retained only 34% (287/843) of households in Mudaka and 58% (513/890) in Panzi and excluded households with missing baseline cluster variables or village data, undermining representativeness of the analyzed sample.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 3 (Methods: Study setting); PDF Pages 4-5 (Methods: Market segmentation analysis; Results: Mudaka, Panzi)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.2: Are measurements appropriate regarding both the outcome and intervention (or exposure)?
domain_ratings.justification: Although baseline socioeconomic indicators used pretested DHS modules, intended primary child morbidity outcomes (14-day diarrhea, cough, fever, and chart records) failed due to poor maternal recall and inaccessible medical charts and were dropped, while the primary service utilization/exposure classification suffered from respondent confusion between 'Asili member' and 'Asili user'.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.3: Are there complete outcome data?
domain_ratings.justification: Outcome data were severely incomplete: 66% of baseline households in Mudaka (556/843) and 42% in Panzi (377/890) were lost to follow-up, and child morbidity outcome data were completely excluded due to poor quality.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 (Methods: Outcomes; Results: Mudaka); PDF Page 5 (Results: Panzi); PDF Page 7 (Limitations)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.4: Are the confounders accounted for in the design and analysis?
domain_ratings.justification: No confounders were controlled for in either study design or statistical analysis; sites were analyzed separately without a comparator arm using only unadjusted descriptive proportions and exploratory k-means clustering without multivariable adjustment.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 (Methods: Data analysis); PDF Page 6 (Discussion)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.5: During the study period, is the intervention administered (or exposure occurred) as intended?
domain_ratings.justification: In Panzi, the authors report 'longer-than-expected service roll-out times, which were beyond the control of the research team', compressing follow-up to 5-8 months, and no objective operational fidelity metrics (water uptime, water quality, or clinic staffing/stockouts) are reported.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 3 (Methods: Data collection, Fig. 1); PDF Page 7 (Limitations)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper does not articulate an explicit methodological rationale for combining quantitative surveys and qualitative focus groups, stating only that 'additional community input was collected through small focus groups during follow-up'.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: In both site-specific Results sections and the Discussion, quantitative k-means market segmentation trends showing lower Asili usage in poorer clusters are directly integrated with focus group quotes explaining that clinic and standpipe user fees deterred low-income families.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors coherently synthesize quantitative utilization disparities and qualitative affordability narratives to conclude that uniform cost-recovery pricing limits reach in impoverished conflict zones and that tiered SES pricing or social-return-on-investment models may be needed.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 1 (Abstract: Conclusions); PDF Pages 6-7 (Discussion, Conclusion)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Potential tensions—such as very low formal Asili membership (1% in Panzi, 6% in Mudaka) versus moderate self-reported usership (43-46%) and positive qualitative claims of child health improvement despite unusable quantitative morbidity data—are noted under Limitations (respondent confusion over 'member' vs. 'user' and recall issues) rather than systematically reconciled across strands.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Neither strand meets the methodological quality standards of its tradition: the quantitative component suffers from 42-66% attrition, omitted primary morbidity outcomes, exposure/outcome misclassification ('member' vs. 'user'), and unadjusted exploratory clustering, while the qualitative component omits basic reporting of focus group sample size, recruitment, data collection, and coding methods.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 3-7 (Methods, Results, Limitations, Author contributions)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Behl et al. (2022) conducted a primary mixed-methods pre-post evaluation of the Asili social enterprise program (small-format primary care clinics and clean water standpipes) in two conflict-affected communities (Mudaka and Panzi) in South Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo. Appraised using the MMAT (2018), overall methodological quality is low (high methodological concern), as MMAT guidance stipulates that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component. While the study productively integrates exploratory quantitative k-means market segmentation of household wealth proxies with qualitative focus group insights to show that user fees limited Asili uptake among poorer households, both empirical strands exhibit major limitations. Quantitatively, the study was retrospectively registered (NCT03536286) near follow-up, suffered severe longitudinal attrition (66% loss in Mudaka; 42% loss in Panzi), dropped its intended primary child morbidity outcomes entirely due to poor maternal recall and unavailable clinic charts, relied on self-reported Asili membership/usage affected by respondent confusion between 'member' and 'user', selectively omitted baseline water/sanitation cluster variables lacking 'notable trends', and performed no control-group or multivariable confounder adjustment. Qualitatively, the Methods section omits the number of focus groups, participant selection criteria, interview guides, recording/transcription procedures, and formal coding methodology.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern / Low overall quality (per MMAT 2018 guidance, no numeric composite score is computed and overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component: all five Quantitative non-randomized items are rated No [4] or Can't tell [1], three of five Qualitative items are rated Can't tell, and two Mixed-Methods items including 5.5 are rated No)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Mixed-methods longitudinal pre-post program evaluation combining household surveys (descriptive stratification and exploratory k-means market segmentation clustering) with follow-up community focus group discussions
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, setting, sampling, survey/focus group collection, dropped child morbidity outcomes, and k-means clustering methods on PDF Pages 1 and 3-4; site retention rates, market segmentation results, and focus group quotes on PDF Pages 4-6; attrition, rollout delay, recall, and member-vs-user misclassification limitations plus author analytic roles on PDF Page 7.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper collects, analyzes, and integrates both primary quantitative empirical data (pre- and post-rollout household surveys with N=843/287 in Mudaka and N=890/513 in Panzi analyzed via descriptive statistics and k-means market segmentation) and primary qualitative empirical data (follow-up community focus group discussions translated and analyzed to explain service utilization and cost barriers). Because it is a genuine mixed-methods primary empirical evaluation of a non-randomized community intervention (registered as NCT03536286) examining associations between baseline household socioeconomic profiles and subsequent Asili uptake alongside qualitative focus groups, the MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) using the Quantitative non-randomized block (3.1-3.5) is the exact matching checklist under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
